title: My Demo is on Steam! Built in Godot with the help of Ai Tools.
author: boneheadlabs
selftext:
I've been solo-developing **Apple Man Sam** in **Godot** for about six months and am excited to announce the demo is now available! If you're an aspiring game dev check it out and see what can be accomplished with our favourite tools.

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/4293080/Apple\_Man\_Sam/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4293080/Apple_Man_Sam/)

Ai tools have played a key role in development of the game's code in the **Godot** game engine. I have made use of several tools including Cursor, Windsurf, Codex and most recently Claude code.

Developing the game this way has been an experience in both learning **how games are architectected and optimised** and **how to get AI to do things correctly.** Over this Journey I have learned a lot but here are a few key tips on the **Programming Side** of Ai game dev.

1. **Learn the underlying language** (in my case gdscript), you can get quite far without this tip, but you will inevitably hit a sticking point where you need to understand what the LLM is trying to do, there were several points where I would be stuck in a loop of a repeated mistake, and need to be able to clearly explain what to change.

2. **Learn game architecture and optimisation** , there are decades of experience to leverage and it is worth the time to learn, even if you aren't implementing it line by line yourself, being able to ask for systems to be architected in an optimal way was a lesson I learned the hard way. the initial architecture of this game produced a 12fps floor, as it was not built fit for purpose. Learning how games like **Vampire Survivors** were architected in the backend allowed me to ask the LLM to rearchitect in an optimal way, and boost that fps floor to a 120fps floor.

3. **Playtest often and with care.** This is probably the biggest tip, especially for complex projects and not just prototypes. Developing with AI is effectively creating hundreds of small pieces of software in isolation and stitching them together, in spite of using best practices like guardrail documents and centralisation of systems, your LLM will often take different approaches to the same problem.  
It will also couple together components you wouldn't have expected.  
So, asking for a change that affects multiple pieces can easily break something that was reliably working for a long time. Spend some of the time saved by using LLMs testing often and testing carefully.  
Enabling your AI to assist you in testing can also help with this, in my case I have a shell script that executes test scenes with extended debugging and logs, which the LLM can assess and adjust accordingly.

If you're interested in more details, I often run dev streams on twitch where I would be happy to chat with anyone keen to learn more. I also make youtube videos!
